LINQ stands for **L**anguage **I**ntegrated **Q**uery.

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
LINQ is a set of extension methods and some special C# syntax that simplifies the work with collections.

LINQ allows to do things like filtering items in collection, projecting them to new forms or aggregating items in a concise syntax. All of these things can also be accomplished using simple loops and temporary variables, but the need to do that is so frequent, that it warrants a standard library for this purpose.
:::

***

```{.csharp}
// Sample data set to be used throughout the lecture

class Person
{
    public string FirstName { get; set; }
    public string LastName { get; set; }
    public int Age { get; set; }

    public override string ToString() => $"{FirstName} {LastName} ({Age})";
}

var data = new List<Person>
{
    new Person { FirstName = "John", LastName = "Doe", Age = 25 },
    new Person { FirstName = "Jane", LastName = "Doe", Age = 26 },
    new Person { FirstName = "John", LastName = "Smith", Age = 30 },
    new Person { FirstName = "Jane", LastName = "Smith", Age = 31 },
    new Person { FirstName = "John", LastName = "Johnson", Age = 35 },
    new Person { FirstName = "Jane", LastName = "Johnson", Age = 36 },
    new Person { FirstName = "John", LastName = "Williams", Age = 40 },
    new Person { FirstName = "Jane", LastName = "Williams", Age = 41 },
    new Person { FirstName = "John", LastName = "Brown", Age = 45 },
    new Person { FirstName = "Jane", LastName = "Brown", Age = 46 },
    new Person { FirstName = "Anthony", LastName = "Davis", Age = 50 },
    new Person { FirstName = "Jessica", LastName = "Davis", Age = 51 },
    new Person { FirstName = "Michael", LastName = "Davis", Age = 55 },
    new Person { FirstName = "Michelle", LastName = "Davis", Age = 56 },
    new Person { FirstName = "David", LastName = "Davis", Age = 60 },
    new Person { FirstName = "Danielle", LastName = "Davis", Age = 61 },
    new Person { FirstName = "Daniel", LastName = "Davis", Age = 65 },
    new Person { FirstName = "Diana", LastName = "Davis", Age = 66 },
    new Person { FirstName = "Dennis", LastName = "Davis", Age = 70 },
};
```

## The problem

Let's say we wanted to get all people from dataset, whose first name starts with the letter "D". An obvious approach would be to iterate through the collection, run some predicate on the items, and move items that match the predicate to some separate collection.

```{.csharp}
var results = new List<Person>();

foreach (var person in data)
{
    if (person.FirstName.StartsWith("D"))
    {
        results.Add(person);
    }
}

results.DisplayTable();
```

***

Similarly, the average age of the people in the list can be calculated.

```{.csharp}
var ageTotal = 0;

foreach (var person in data)
{
    ageTotal += person.Age;
}

// Without the cast this would be an integer division, silently returning 46
var averageAge = (double)ageTotal / data.Count;

averageAge.Display();
```

***

Or concatenate the names of all the persons in data set.

```{.csharp}
var allNames = String.Empty;

foreach (var person in data)
{
    allNames += $"{person.FirstName} {person.LastName}, ";
}

allNames = allNames.TrimEnd(',', ' ');

allNames.Display();
```

***

The common pattern can be seen:

1. Define some variable to accumulate the results.
2. Check if the item in the collection matches the predicate.
3. Update the result accumulator.

Looking at the code, most of it is identical except a few custom bits.

## Using the LINQ

All of the LINQ methods are generic and will be type safe. This is needed to be able to reliably write predicates or projections.

All of the LINQ extension methods reside in `System.Linq` namespace.

### `.Where()`

`.Where()` method takes in a predicate and returns the items of the original collection that match the given predicate.

```{.csharp}
// Same example where we check if the first name starts with "D" using LINQ

data.Where(p => p.FirstName.StartsWith("D")).DisplayTable();
```

### `.Select()`

`.Select()` method is used to project data in the collection to a different form.

```{.csharp}
// Select all names from data collection into concatenated strings

data.Select(p => $"{p.FirstName} {p.LastName}").DisplayTable();
```

### `.SelectMany()`

`.SelectMany()` method is used to flatten the results. It works similarly to how `.Select()` works in terms of projecting the item form, but also performs flattening at the same time. Flattening in this case means reducing the dimensions of the collection. I.e. if the item inside collection has another collection inside of it, flattening would extract the items from nested collection and place all these items into single collection.

```{.csharp}
class InnerCollection
{
    public List<int> Numbers { get; set; }
}

class OuterCollection
{
    public List<InnerCollection> Items { get; set; }
}

var outerCollection = new OuterCollection
    {
        Items = new List<InnerCollection>
        {
            new InnerCollection { Numbers = new List<int> { 1, 2, 3 } },
            new InnerCollection { Numbers = new List<int> { 4, 5, 6 } },
        },
    };

var flatNumbers = outerCollection.Items.SelectMany(i => i.Numbers);

flatNumbers.Display();
```

### `.Aggregate()`

`.Aggregate()` method reduces the values in a collection into a single one.

In its simplest form `.Aggregate()` takes in a `Func` of 2 arguments as its argument: 1st argument holds the aggregated value and the 2nd argument holds the current item from the data set.

```{.csharp}
// Calculate the sum age of all persons in the data collection.
// Without a seed, the aggregated value is of the same type as the items,
// so the ages are projected to int by Select'ing them first.
data.Select(x => x.Age).Aggregate((x, y) => x + y).Display();
```

***

```{.csharp}
// With a seed (initial value), the aggregated value can be of any type.
data.Aggregate(0, (sum, person) => sum + person.Age).Display();

data.Aggregate("", (names, person) => names + person.FirstName[0]).Display();
```

### Other aggregates

Similarly to `.Aggregate()`, there are various other aggregate methods for the most common use cases like sum, average etc.

```{.csharp}
// Calculate the sum of all ages in the data collection.
data.Sum(p => p.Age).Display();

// Calculate the average age of all persons in the data collection.
data.Average(p => p.Age).Display();

// Calculate the maximum age of all persons in the data collection.
data.Max(p => p.Age).Display();

// Calculate the minimum age of all persons in the data collection.
data.Min(p => p.Age).Display();

// Count the persons matching the predicate.
data.Count(p => p.LastName == "Davis").Display();
```

***

```{.csharp}
// Max and Min return the value itself,
// while MaxBy and MinBy (.NET 6+) return the item that has that value.
data.MaxBy(p => p.Age).Display();
data.MinBy(p => p.Age).Display();
```

### `.Any()` and `.All()`

`.Any()` method returns a boolean that indicates if any of the elements in the collection match the given predicate. `.All()` method returns a boolean that indicates if all the elements in the collection match the given predicate.

```{.csharp}
// Check if anyone in the collection is over the age of 90.
data.Any(p => p.Age > 90).Display();
```

***

```{.csharp}
// Check if everyone in the collection is over the age of 18.
data.All(p => p.Age > 18).Display();
```

***

```{.csharp}
// Check if everyone in the collection is over the age of 50.
data.All(p => p.Age > 50).Display();
```

### Ordering

`.OrderBy()` and `.OrderByDescending()` sort the collection by the given key. `.ThenBy()` and `.ThenByDescending()` add further keys for the items whose previous keys are equal.

```{.csharp}
// Order by last name, then the oldest first within the same last name.
data
    .OrderBy(p => p.LastName)
    .ThenByDescending(p => p.Age)
    .DisplayTable();
```

### `.GroupBy()`

`.GroupBy()` allows to group the collection into several subgroups based on the given expression. Grouping the collection results in a collection of collections, with each of them having an additional `.Key` property that indicates the value by which it was grouped.

```{.csharp}
// Group the data by the first name of the person.
// Each group is a collection of persons with an additional Key property.
data
    .GroupBy(x => x.FirstName)
    .Select(g => $"{g.Key}: {string.Join(", ", g.Select(p => p.LastName))}")
    .DisplayTable();
```

***

```{.csharp}
// Group by, as well as any other LINQ method, can be chained, to get more specific results.
data
    .GroupBy(x => x.FirstName)
    .Select(x => new { FirstName = x.Key, Count = x.Count() })
    .OrderByDescending(x => x.Count)
    .ThenBy(x => x.FirstName)
    .DisplayTable();
```

### Other useful methods

```{.csharp}
// Distinct removes duplicates, DistinctBy (.NET 6+) removes items with duplicate keys.
data.Select(p => p.LastName).Distinct().Display();
data.DistinctBy(p => p.LastName).Display();
```

***

```{.csharp}
// Chunk (.NET 6+) splits the collection into chunks of the given size.
data.Select(p => p.Age).Chunk(5).Select(chunk => string.Join(", ", chunk)).DisplayTable();
```

***

```{.csharp}
// CountBy (.NET 9+) is a shortcut for GroupBy + Count.
data.CountBy(p => p.LastName).Display();

// ToDictionary materializes the collection into a dictionary with the given key.
var byName = data.ToDictionary(p => $"{p.FirstName} {p.LastName}");
byName["Diana Davis"].Display();
```

### Selecting single element out of the collection

There are a few options how to select single element out of the collection:

- `First()` takes the first element out, throws if there are no elements.
- `FirstOrDefault()` takes the first element out or the default value for the type if there are no elements in the collection.
- `Single()` takes the single element out of the collection, throws if the element count in collection is different than 1.
- `SingleOrDefault()` takes the single element out of the collection if there is only 1, returns the default value for the type if there are none, throws if there are more than 1 element in the collection.
- `Last()` and `LastOrDefault()` work like `First()` and `FirstOrDefault()`, but from the end.

All of them also have an overload that takes a predicate, which works like `.Where(predicate)` followed by the method.

***

```{.csharp}
// First usage examples
Console.WriteLine(data.First());
Console.WriteLine(data.First(p => p.Age > 50));
Console.WriteLine(data.Last());
```

***

```{.csharp}
// First but the collection is empty
Console.WriteLine(new List<Person>().First());
```

***

```{.csharp}
// FirstOrDefault on the empty collection.
// The default value of a reference type is null.
Console.WriteLine(new List<Person>().FirstOrDefault() is null);
```

***

```{.csharp}
// Single with a predicate matching exactly one element
Console.WriteLine(data.Single(p => p.FirstName == "Dennis"));
```

***

```{.csharp}
// Single on the empty collection
Console.WriteLine(new List<Person>().Single());
```

***

```{.csharp}
// SingleOrDefault on the empty collection
Console.WriteLine(new List<Person>().SingleOrDefault() is null);
```

***

```{.csharp}
// SingleOrDefault on the collection with more than one element
Console.WriteLine(data.SingleOrDefault());
```

### `.Take()` and `.Skip()`

`.Take()` selects first `n` items from the given collection.

Similarly `.Skip()` skips over first `n` elements from the collection. It is typically used in conjunction with `.Take()` to implement things like pagination.

***

```{.csharp}
// Skip the first 2 elements, then take the next 5.

var orderedByName = data
    .OrderBy(p => p.FirstName)
    .ThenBy(p => p.LastName);

orderedByName.DisplayTable();

var skippedAndTaken = orderedByName
    .Skip(2)
    .Take(5);

skippedAndTaken.DisplayTable();
```

## Deferred execution

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
Most LINQ methods that return a collection (`Where`, `Select`, `OrderBy`, ...) do not do any work when called. They only describe the query, which is executed when the result is enumerated - with `foreach`, or by methods like `ToList()`, `Count()` or `First()`. This is called deferred (or lazy) execution.
:::

```{.csharp}
var numbers = new List<int> { 1, 2, 3 };

// Nothing is filtered yet, the query is only defined
var bigNumbers = numbers.Where(n => n > 1);

numbers.Add(4);

// The query runs now, so it sees the number added after it was defined
Console.WriteLine(string.Join(", ", bigNumbers));
```

***

```{.csharp}
// The query runs again on every enumeration
var evaluations = 0;
var query = numbers.Where(n => { evaluations++; return n > 1; });

query.Count();
query.Count();
Console.WriteLine($"Evaluations without ToList: {evaluations}");

// ToList (or ToArray) runs the query once and stores the results
evaluations = 0;
var materialized = query.ToList();
materialized.Count();
materialized.Count();
Console.WriteLine($"Evaluations with ToList: {evaluations}");
```

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
Enumerating the same query several times is a common source of bugs and performance issues, especially when the query is expensive (e.g. reads a file or a database). When the results are needed more than once, materialize them with `ToList()` or `ToArray()`.
:::

## `IEnumerable<T>` and `IQueryable<T>`

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
LINQ methods on `IEnumerable<T>` take delegates (`Func<T, bool>`), which are compiled code executed in memory. LINQ methods on `IQueryable<T>` take expression trees (`Expression<Func<T, bool>>`), which are data describing the code. A LINQ provider, like Entity Framework Core, can inspect the expression tree and translate it to something else, for example SQL. The lambda looks the same in both cases, the compiler decides what to produce based on the target type.
:::

```{.csharp}
using System.Linq.Expressions;

// The same lambda can be compiled into a delegate, or into an expression tree
Func<Person, bool> compiled = p => p.Age > 30;
Expression<Func<Person, bool>> expression = p => p.Age > 30;

// A delegate can only be invoked
Console.WriteLine(compiled(data[0]));

// An expression tree can be inspected
Console.WriteLine(expression);
Console.WriteLine(expression.Body.NodeType);
```

***

```csharp
// IQueryable: the filter is translated to SQL and runs in the database
// SELECT ... FROM Students WHERE Age > 30
var inDatabase = dbContext.Students.Where(s => s.Age > 30).ToList();

// IEnumerable: all students are loaded into memory, then filtered
var inMemory = dbContext.Students.AsEnumerable().Where(s => s.Age > 30).ToList();
```

## Query syntax

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
The examples above used the extension method syntax. However C# also has the special query syntax for LINQ usage. It has SQL-like syntax, which is said to be more readable and self explanatory than extension method syntax. The assumption is that it should be easier to read a LINQ statement written in query syntax compared to extension method syntax.

However query syntax is very different from the typical syntax seen in C-like languages, so it tends to look out of place. Query syntax also has more limitations than extension method syntax, because it has fewer methods to choose from, so in more complex scenarios it has to be used in conjunction with extension method syntax. Also because it is more verbose, it tends to take more code to achieve the same result.
:::

```{.csharp}
// Filter the persons whose name starts with "J" and age is greater than 30.

var results =
    from person in data
    where person.FirstName.StartsWith("J") && person.Age > 30
    select person;

results.DisplayTable();
```

***

```{.csharp}
// Select the max age of the person whose name starts with "J".
// Since there is no Max in query syntax, it leads to a mixed usage of query and method syntax.

var maxAge =
    (from person in data
    where person.FirstName.StartsWith("J")
    select person.Age).Max();

maxAge.Display();
```

***

```{.csharp}
// Group the data by the last name of the person,
// then select the first person in each group,
// then select the first name of the person,
// but only of the people whose age is greater than 30.

var results =
    from person in data
    group person by person.LastName into g
    select g.First() into firstPerson
    where firstPerson.Age > 30
    select firstPerson.FirstName;

results.DisplayTable();
```

## Homemade LINQ

In this section we will explore an example how to create extension methods that provide similar functionality to the standard LINQ methods.

```{.csharp}
// All the methods are generic, so they would work with any type, while providing type safety.
// All the methods are extension methods.
// Arguments are Funcs, since they are either projection or predicate functions.
// Methods should return enumerables, where appropriate, so they could be chained.
// yield return makes the method lazy: its body only runs when the result is enumerated.

public static IEnumerable<T> Where<T>(
    this IEnumerable<T> source,
    Func<T, bool> predicate)
{
    Console.WriteLine("Where called");

    foreach (var item in source)
    {
        if (predicate(item))
        {
            yield return item;
        }
    }
}
```

***

```{.csharp}
// Select works the same way, just projecting instead of filtering.
public static IEnumerable<TTarget> Select<TSource, TTarget>(
    this IEnumerable<TSource> source,
    Func<TSource, TTarget> projection)
{
    Console.WriteLine("Select called");

    foreach (var item in source)
    {
        yield return projection(item);
    }
}
```

***

```{.csharp}
// FirstOrDefault returns a single value instead of a collection, so it does not use yield
// and its body runs immediately.
public static T FirstOrDefault<T>(
    this IEnumerable<T> source,
    Func<T, bool> predicate)
{
    Console.WriteLine("FirstOrDefault called");

    foreach (var item in source)
    {
        if (predicate(item))
        {
            return item;
        }
    }

    return default(T);
}
```

***

```{.csharp}
// In this script the methods declared above take precedence over System.Linq.
// In a regular project they would be declared in a static class, and importing its namespace
// together with System.Linq would make the calls ambiguous (error CS0121).

data.Where(p => p.FirstName.StartsWith("D")).DisplayTable();
```

***

```{.csharp}
// Building the query does not print anything, because Where and Select use yield.
var query = data.Where(x => x.Age > 30).Select(x => x.FirstName);
Console.WriteLine("Query built");

// FirstOrDefault runs immediately and starts enumerating Select,
// which in turn starts enumerating Where - so the calls are printed in reverse order.
var first = query.FirstOrDefault(name => name.StartsWith("J"));
Console.WriteLine(first);
```

## Exercises to try out LINQ

Using the `data` list defined at the beginning of the lecture and LINQ extension methods, try doing the exercises below.

*It may not be possible to complete every single exercise with absolutely pure single statement LINQ.*

1. Find the most common last name.
2. Find the person whose first name and last name together are the longest.
3. Find the oldest person by each last name.
4. Check if there is more than 1 person of the same age.
5. Check if there is more than 1 person with the same first and last name combination.
6. Find the average last name length.
7. Return the `{FirstName} {LastName}` of the people with top 3 oldest ages (assume that there can be multiple people of the same age).
8. Find the second oldest person.
9. Calculate the occurrences of letters in people's names.
10. Construct the string of 5 most common first name letters ordered descending.
